title: Driving Technique
intro: Knowing the line is half the job; the other half is the inputs that keep the car on it at the limit. This page covers braking, turning in, using the throttle, shifting gears, catching slides and where to look. The aim throughout is the same: keep the tyres working near their peak grip for as much of the lap as possible, and never ask them for more than they have.

blocks.text: Every input moves weight around the car (see #/racing/vehicle-dynamics). A sudden input moves it suddenly, the tyres are overloaded for a moment, they slide past their peak, and grip is lost. A smooth input lets the load arrive gradually and the tyres follow it. Smooth does not mean slow: the best drivers make large, fast inputs, but they build them up and release them progressively, with no jerks or corrections.

items: Threshold braking: braking as hard as the tyres allow without locking the wheels. The pedal goes on hard and fast at first, while weight is moving onto the front tyres and they can take more, then the pressure is eased as the car slows (aerodynamic downforce falls with speed, so a high-downforce car needs less pedal as it slows).
Locking a wheel: a locked tyre slides at near zero grip for steering and somewhat less grip for stopping, and flat-spots the tyre. The cure is to release a little pressure and reapply.

ABS (anti-lock braking) prevents locking by pulsing the brake pressure. Many race cars and most road cars have it; in games it is often an assist that can be turned on or off. With ABS the driver can press harder without fear of locking, but should still brake firmly and release smoothly rather than stamp on the pedal and wait, because the car still needs grip left over to turn in.

Braking points: start conservative and move the braking point a few metres later each lap until the car can no longer make the corner, then back off one step. Braking later only helps if the car still makes the apex.

blocks.text: Trail braking means carrying some brake pressure past the turn-in point and releasing it gradually as the steering goes on, instead of finishing all the braking in a straight line. It does two things. It keeps the tyres on the edge of the friction circle as the job changes from braking to cornering, so no grip is wasted. And it keeps load on the front tyres while they start the turn, which helps the car rotate. Too much brake while turning overloads the front and the car understeers, or unloads the rear and the car oversteers. The release is the skill: as steering goes up, brake comes down, so the total demand on the tyres stays about constant.

items: Maintenance throttle: in the middle of a corner, a little throttle balances the car and keeps weight from moving forward. Abruptly lifting mid-corner can cause lift-off oversteer.

Exit: squeeze the throttle on progressively as the steering unwinds. The rule many coaches teach is that the steering and throttle should mirror each other: the more steering lock, the less throttle; as the steering straightens, the throttle goes down.

Wheelspin and traction control: too much throttle, especially in low gears, makes the driven tyres spin; in a rear-driven car the rear then slides out. Traction control cuts power to stop it. Without it, a driver modulates the pedal, or short-shifts (changes up early) to send less torque to the wheels.
Commitment: once at full throttle on exit, stay there. Lifting and reapplying on the straight costs speed for its whole length.

blocks.text: Most power comes near the top of the rev range, so on a straight the driver shifts up near the limiter (or wherever the engine's power curve says the next gear gives more force at the wheels). On the way into a corner the driver changes down while braking so that the right gear is ready for the exit. A downshift spins the engine faster, so to avoid a jolt that locks or unsettles the driven wheels, the driver blips the throttle to match the revs (rev matching). In a car with a clutch and an H-pattern gearbox, doing this while braking needs heel-and-toe: the ball of the right foot on the brake and the heel or side of the foot on the throttle. Modern sequential and paddle-shift gearboxes often blip automatically, and many games do it for the player.

items: Turn in once, with one smooth movement to roughly the lock the corner needs, rather than winding in more and more as the corner goes on.
Every steering correction mid-corner is a sign the turn-in was wrong: too early, too fast or with too little speed scrubbed off.
Hands: keep both hands on the wheel, at roughly the nine and three o'clock positions, so the wheel's centre is always known and the force feedback can be felt clearly.
Less steering is often faster: a tyre past its peak slip angle makes less force, so more lock can make an understeering car turn less. Unwinding a little lets the front tyres grip again.

Oversteer: steer into the slide (point the front wheels where the car is going, also called opposite lock or counter-steering) and ease, but do not snap off, the throttle. The quicker and smaller the correction, the better. Unwind the counter-steer as the rear grips, or the car will snap the other way (tank-slapper).
Understeer: do not add more steering. Reduce the steering a little and ease the throttle (or a light brake) to bring weight onto the front tyres so they grip again.
Spinning: if the car is going to spin, both feet in (brake and clutch) so the car slides in a straight line, which makes its path predictable to other drivers.

blocks.text: Look where you want to go, not where you are. At the braking point the driver's eyes should already be on the turn-in point, at turn-in on the apex, and at the apex on the exit. The hands follow the eyes. Looking far ahead also makes speed feel slower, which leaves more time to react. In a simulator, a correct field of view (see #/racing/practice-and-data) makes distances and speeds look as they would from a real seat.

A driver who can repeat the same lap time within a tenth of a second can then change one thing and see whether it helped. A driver who varies by a second cannot learn anything from a single lap. Build speed in steps: learn the line, then brake later, then carry more speed to the apex, then get on the throttle earlier.

The order of priorities in a corner for most drivers: get the braking done right, get the car pointed at the right apex, then get on the throttle as early as possible. A good exit beats a heroic entry.

Sources: Smith, C. (1996), Drive to Win, Carroll Smith Consulting. Bentley, R. (1998), Speed Secrets, Motorbooks. Lopez, C. (2001), Going Faster! Mastering the Art of Race Driving, Bentley Publishers. Krumm, M. (2011), Driving on the Edge: The Art and Science of Race Driving, Icon Publishing.
